lessons.title: Atoms, Elements and the Development of the Atomic Model

practice_questions.text: Define the term 'isotope'.
practice_questions.marks: Atoms of the same element that have the same number of protons (same atomic number) but different numbers of neutrons (different mass numbers). Accept: same element, different mass number.

practice_questions.text: An atom of fluorine has atomic number 9 and mass number 19. State the number of protons, neutrons and electrons in this atom.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark: 9 protons. 1 mark: 10 neutrons (19 − 9). 1 mark: 9 electrons (equals number of protons in a neutral atom).

practice_questions.text: Boron has two naturally occurring isotopes: boron-10 (20% abundance) and boron-11 (80% abundance). Calculate the relative atomic mass of boron. Show your working.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark: Correct calculation: (20 × 10 + 80 × 11) ÷ 100 = (200 + 880) ÷ 100 = 1080 ÷ 100. 1 mark: Final answer 10.8 (no unit required for relative atomic mass).

practice_questions.text: Describe Rutherford's gold foil experiment and explain how the results disproved the plum pudding model of the atom.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Describes alpha particles fired at thin gold foil; detector records deflections; most pass straight through (atom is mostly empty space); a small number are deflected at large angles (positively charged nucleus repels positive alpha particles); very few bounce back (nucleus is very dense and small); plum pudding model predicted only slight deflections; the result disproved it because a diffuse positive charge could not cause large deflections; new nuclear model proposed with dense central nucleus.
Secure: Describes the experiment and links at least two observations to conclusions about atomic structure.
Developing: Describes the experiment and states that the result led to the nuclear model, with one observational link.
Emerging: Describes the experiment broadly without connecting results to model change.

practice_questions.text: Explain why Dalton's claim that 'all atoms of an element are identical' is an oversimplification.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark: Isotopes of the same element exist — they have the same number of protons but different numbers of neutrons. 1 mark: Isotopes therefore have the same atomic number but different mass numbers, meaning atoms of the same element are not identical in mass.

practice_questions.text: Evaluate how the discovery of the electron and the neutron each contributed to improving scientific models of the atom. Refer to named scientists in your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Discusses Thomson's discovery of the electron (1897) and resulting plum pudding model — strength: first evidence of internal structure; limitation: failed to account for the concentrated nucleus; Rutherford's gold foil experiment (1909–1911) replaced it with the nuclear model; Chadwick's discovery of the neutron (1932) — explained mass discrepancy and the existence of isotopes; evaluates how each discovery was driven by new experimental evidence; discusses how each model improved on the last; considers whether science ever produces a 'complete' model; justified conclusion.
Secure: Named scientists, their discoveries, and how each refined the model, with evaluative reasoning and a conclusion.
Developing: Names at least three scientists and their contributions with limited evaluation.
Emerging: Lists scientists without explaining how their discoveries changed models.

practice_questions.text: State why Mendeleev left gaps in his periodic table.
practice_questions.marks: He predicted that elements had yet to be discovered that would fill the gaps (and whose properties would match predictions based on their position in the table).

practice_questions.text: Write the electronic configuration of phosphorus (atomic number 15) and identify which group and period it is in.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark: Electronic configuration 2, 8, 5. 1 mark: Group 5 (5 outer electrons). 1 mark: Period 3 (3 electron shells occupied).

practice_questions.text: Explain why the reactivity of Group 1 metals increases going down the group.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Group 1 metals all have one electron in their outer shell; going down the group the outer shell is in an energy level further from the nucleus; the electrostatic attraction between the nucleus and the outer electron decreases; the electron is more easily lost; so the metal reacts more readily (is more reactive).
Secure: Three of the four points above with correct causal language.
Developing: States reactivity increases and mentions the outer electron being further from the nucleus without explaining attraction.
Emerging: States reactivity increases going down Group 1 only.

practice_questions.text: Chlorine water is added to a solution of potassium iodide. Describe and explain what you would observe, writing a symbol equation for the reaction.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark: The solution turns brown/dark orange. 1 mark: Iodine is produced — chlorine is more reactive than iodine and displaces it from the potassium iodide solution. 1 mark: Cl₂ + 2KI → 2KCl + I₂ (allow word equation for this mark). 1 mark: Chlorine gains electrons more easily than iodine (its outer shell is closer to the nucleus, so it has a stronger pull on incoming electrons).

practice_questions.text: Compare the properties of Group 1 metals with those of transition metals.
practice_questions.marks: Any four correct comparative points, one mark each: Group 1 are highly reactive / transition metals are much less reactive; Group 1 have low melting points / transition metals have high melting points; Group 1 are soft and low density / transition metals are hard and high density; Group 1 form colourless ionic compounds / transition metals form coloured compounds; transition metals (not Group 1) commonly act as catalysts.

practice_questions.text: Evaluate the significance of Mendeleev's periodic table in the development of chemistry as a science. Refer to specific features of his table and how later discoveries confirmed or challenged his ideas.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Explains the historical context (elements classified by atomic weight before Mendeleev); evaluates Mendeleev's specific innovations (ordering by atomic weight, grouping by properties, gaps for undiscovered elements, swapping element positions); discusses the predictive success (gallium, germanium predicted before discovery and later confirmed); discusses how later work (discovery of atomic number and subatomic particles) refined rather than overturned his table; considers limitations (no explanation of why similar elements have similar properties — required electron theory); justified conclusion about the table's scientific importance.
Secure: Covers at least three features of Mendeleev's table, how predictions were confirmed and how the modern table differs, with a conclusion.
Developing: Describes Mendeleev's table and gaps for undiscovered elements with limited evaluation.
Emerging: Describes Mendeleev's contribution with few specific details.

before.exam_tip_html: Two classic errors to avoid in periodic table questions: (1) saying “reactivity increases down Group 7” — it decreases because it becomes harder to gain an electron; (2) confusing groups and periods — groups are vertical columns (same outer electrons), periods are horizontal rows (same number of shells). For displacement reactions, you must state which halogen is more reactive and explain why the displacement does (or does not) occur. Show the word equation or symbol equation for full marks on 3-mark calculation questions about electronic configurations.

before.content_html:
Ionic Bonding

When a metal reacts with a non-metal, electrons are transferred from the metal atom to the non-metal atom. The metal atom loses one or more electrons to form a positive ion (cation), and the non-metal atom gains those electrons to become a negative ion (anion). Both ions then have full outer electron shells and are stable.

The strong electrostatic attraction between the oppositely charged ions is called an ionic bond. In sodium chloride (NaCl), sodium loses one electron to become \(Na^+\) and chlorine gains one electron to become \(Cl^-\). The resulting ions pack together in a regular three-dimensional arrangement called a giant ionic lattice.

Key Fact

Ionic bonding: metal atoms lose electrons (form positive ions) and non-metal atoms gain electrons (form negative ions). Strong electrostatic attraction between the opposite charges holds ions together in a giant ionic lattice.

Naming Ionic Compounds

The name of an ionic compound gives useful information about which ions are present. When a metal combines with a non-metal element only, the non-metal ion takes an -ide ending — for example, sodium chloride, magnesium oxide, potassium iodide. When the compound contains oxygen as part of a polyatomic ion, it usually takes an -ate ending — for example, sodium sulfate, copper(II) nitrate, calcium carbonate. Recognising these endings tells you instantly whether a simple or complex ion is involved.

Dot-and-cross diagrams show only the outer shell electrons. Use dots for one atom and crosses for the other. For sodium chloride:

  • Draw Na with one outer electron (dot). Draw Cl with seven outer electrons (crosses).
  • Show the dot crossing into Cl's outer shell, so Cl now has eight electrons. Draw square brackets around each ion and write the charge outside: \([Na]^+\) and \([Cl]^-\).

For magnesium oxide, Mg loses two electrons (2,8 → 2,8, 0 becomes \(Mg^{2+}\)) and oxygen gains two (2,6 → 2,8, becomes \(O^{2-}\)).

Covalent Bonding

When non-metals bond with other non-metals, atoms share pairs of electrons rather than transferring them. Each shared pair of electrons is a covalent bond. Both atoms count the shared pair as part of their own outer shell, so both achieve a full, stable electron configuration.

Common examples:

  • \(H_2\) — a single covalent bond (one shared pair).
  • \(O_2\) — a double covalent bond (\(O=O\), two shared pairs).
  • \(H_2O\) — two single covalent bonds (oxygen bonds to two hydrogen atoms).
  • \(CH_4\) — four single covalent bonds (carbon bonds to four hydrogen atoms).
  • \(NH_3\) — three single covalent bonds plus one lone pair on nitrogen.

For water (\(H_2O\)): draw oxygen in the centre with six outer-shell electrons. Draw a hydrogen on each side with one electron. Show one dot from O and one cross from each H overlapping in a shared pair. Each H now has a full shell of two; oxygen has a full shell of eight.

For methane (\(CH_4\)): carbon has four outer electrons. Each of the four hydrogen atoms contributes one electron. Show four shared pairs around carbon, giving it eight; each hydrogen has two.

Only draw outer-shell electrons. Never add electrons that aren't there or remove electrons to make the diagram look neater — the total electron count must balance.

Metallic Bonding

In metals, the outer electrons leave their parent atoms and become delocalised electrons — free to move throughout the entire metal structure. What remains are positive metal ions. The metallic bond is the strong electrostatic attraction between these positive ions and the surrounding sea of electrons.

Key Fact

Metallic bonding: positive metal ions in a lattice surrounded by a sea of delocalised electrons. The electrons carry charge → metals conduct electricity. Layers of ions can slide over each other → metals are malleable and ductile.

Ionic: electrons transferred, metal + non-metal, giant ionic lattice, high melting point, conducts when molten or dissolved.

Covalent: electrons shared, non-metal + non-metal, simple molecules (low m.p.) or giant covalent (very high m.p.), mostly poor conductors.

Metallic: delocalised electrons, metal atoms only, giant metallic lattice, good conductors, malleable, generally high melting points (though mercury is liquid at room temperature).

The key exam skill is justifying properties from structure: ionic compounds have high melting points because many strong electrostatic attractions must be overcome simultaneously. Simple covalent molecules like water have low boiling points because intermolecular forces, not covalent bonds, are broken during boiling. Giant covalent structures like diamond and silicon dioxide have very high melting points because many strong covalent bonds must be broken throughout the entire lattice.

knowledge_checks.q: What type of bonding involves the transfer of electrons from a metal to a non-metal?
In a dot-and-cross diagram for a covalent bond, where are the shared electrons shown?
options: In the overlap region between the two atoms
In the nucleus of one atom

knowledge_checks.q: Which ending tells you that an ionic compound contains a polyatomic ion with oxygen: _____
Why are metals malleable (can be bent and shaped): _____
options: Layers of positive ions can slide over each other in the sea of delocalised electrons
Their outer electrons are tightly held
knowledge_checks.explanation: The correct answer is Layers of positive ions can slide over each other in the sea of delocalised electrons.

before.exam_tip_html: A very common error on 6-mark questions: students say 'covalent bonds break when graphite or diamond melts'. For graphite, the weak intermolecular forces between layers are overcome on melting, not the covalent bonds — this is why graphite still has a very high melting point. For simple molecules, the intermolecular forces are overcome but the covalent bonds within the molecule stay intact. Always name the type of force being overcome, not just 'bonds'. For graphene/fullerenes questions, examiners want the year 1985 (buckminsterfullerene) and 2004 (graphene isolation) — but if unsure, paraphrase: 'discovered in the late twentieth century'.
before.content_html:
Properties of Ionic Compounds

Ionic compounds form giant ionic lattices. The strong electrostatic forces between the ions act in all directions, which gives ionic compounds a characteristic set of properties:

  • High melting and boiling points — a large amount of energy is needed to overcome the many strong bonds acting throughout the lattice.
  • Conduct electricity when molten or dissolved in water — the ions are then free to move and carry charge. They do not conduct when solid because the ions are fixed in position.
  • Brittle — if an external force shifts one layer of ions, identical charges align and repel each other strongly, shattering the crystal.
Key Fact

Ionic compounds: high melting points (strong forces in all directions), conduct when molten or dissolved (ions free to move), do not conduct when solid (ions fixed), brittle (layers shift → repulsion).

Properties of Simple Molecular Substances

Simple molecules (e.g. \(H_2O\), \(CO_2\), \(O_2\)) have strong covalent bonds within the molecule but weak intermolecular forces between molecules. This gives them:

  • Low melting and boiling points — little energy is needed to overcome the weak intermolecular forces (not the covalent bonds themselves).
  • Do not conduct electricity — no free electrons or ions to carry charge.

As molecules get larger, their intermolecular forces become stronger, so boiling points increase with molecular size. This is why large hydrocarbons are liquid or solid at room temperature while small ones (e.g. methane) are gases.

Key Fact

When a simple molecular substance melts or boils, the weak intermolecular forces are overcome — the strong covalent bonds within molecules remain intact. This explains why simple molecules have low melting points despite having strong internal bonds.

Giant Covalent Structures

Giant covalent structures have millions of atoms connected by covalent bonds in a continuous network. They have very high melting points because many strong covalent bonds must be broken to separate the atoms. Examples include diamond, graphite and silicon dioxide.

In diamond, each carbon atom forms four covalent bonds arranged in a rigid tetrahedral pattern. This gives diamond:

  • Extreme hardness — the rigid lattice resists deformation.
  • A very high melting point — all four bonds per atom must be broken.
  • No electrical conductivity — all four outer electrons are used in bonding, leaving none free to carry charge.

In graphite, each carbon atom bonds to three others in flat hexagonal layers. The fourth outer electron from each carbon becomes delocalised — free to move along the layers, allowing graphite to conduct electricity. The layers are held together only by weak intermolecular forces, so they slide easily over one another, making graphite soft and slippery — useful as a lubricant and in pencil leads.

Graphene, Fullerenes and Carbon Nanotubes

Graphene is a single layer of graphite: a one-atom-thick sheet of hexagonally arranged carbon atoms. Scientists Andre Geim and Konstantin Novoselov isolated it at the University of Manchester in 2004, work for which they received the Nobel Prize in Physics in 2010. Graphene is extraordinarily strong relative to its mass and is an excellent conductor of electricity and heat.

Fullerenes are carbon molecules shaped as hollow spheres or tubes. Buckminsterfullerene (\(C_{60}\)) — 60 carbon atoms arranged like a football — was first made in 1985 by Harold Kroto, Robert Curl and Richard Smalley, who were awarded the Nobel Prize in Chemistry in 1996.

Carbon nanotubes are cylindrical fullerenes with remarkable tensile strength and electrical conductivity. They are used in electronics and as reinforcing agents in composite materials.

Key Fact

Diamond: 4 bonds per carbon, rigid, hard, no conductivity. Graphite: 3 bonds per carbon + 1 delocalised electron, layers slide, conducts electricity. Graphene: single graphite layer — isolated 2004, strongest known material per unit mass.

Polymers are very large molecules made from many repeating units called monomers, joined by covalent bonds. Examples include poly(ethene) and poly(propene). The long tangled chains experience stronger intermolecular forces than simple molecules, so polymers are solid at room temperature. They do not conduct electricity and generally have moderate melting points depending on chain length and degree of cross-linking.

When comparing allotropes in the exam, always link structure to property: graphite conducts because delocalised electrons move between layers, whereas diamond does not because all four outer electrons are covalently bonded. Fullerenes and graphene are studied for nanotechnology applications — fullerene cages can carry drug molecules, while graphene's exceptional strength comes from the hexagonal arrangement of carbon atoms in a single layer.

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following correctly explains why graphite conducts electricity?
A) It has a giant ionic lattice with free ions
B) It has delocalised electrons that can move through the layers
C) Its covalent bonds are weak and break easily
D) It has a simple molecular structure
practice_questions.marks: B) It has delocalised electrons that can move through the layers [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: State why ionic compounds conduct electricity when dissolved in water but not when solid.
practice_questions.marks: When dissolved, the ions are free to move and carry charge [1 mark]. When solid, the ions are fixed in the lattice and cannot move [1 mark].

practice_questions.text: A student says: 'When water boils, the covalent bonds break.' Identify the error and give the correct explanation.
practice_questions.marks: Error: it is the weak intermolecular forces between water molecules that are overcome, not the strong covalent O–H bonds [1 mark]. The covalent bonds within the water molecules remain intact when water boils [1 mark].

practice_questions.text: Compare the structure and properties of diamond and graphite, explaining how their different structures lead to their different properties.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (5–6): Diamond — each carbon bonds to four others in a rigid tetrahedral lattice [1], making it very hard [1] and a non-conductor because all electrons are in bonds [1]. Graphite — each carbon bonds to three others in flat hexagonal layers [1], with one delocalised electron per carbon making it a conductor [1], and weak forces between layers make it soft and slippery [1].
Secure (3–4): Correctly explains one allotrope in full, other partially.
Developing (1–2): Mentions '4 bonds' or '3 bonds' but does not link to properties.

practice_questions.text: Buckminsterfullerene (C₆₀) has a molecular formula and structure very different from diamond. Describe the structure of C₆₀ and suggest one potential application.
practice_questions.marks: Structure: 60 carbon atoms [1] arranged in a hollow sphere (like a football) with each carbon bonded to three others [1]. Application: any reasonable suggestion — e.g. drug delivery (the hollow cage can carry molecules), lubricants, or use in electronics [1].

practice_questions.text: 'Graphene is the most useful material discovered in the last 50 years.' Evaluate this claim, referring to the properties of graphene and the limitations of the statement.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (7–9): Properties supporting the claim — graphene is one atom thick, extremely strong per unit mass, and conducts electricity and heat very well [1 per valid property, up to 3]. These make it valuable in electronics, composites and flexible displays [1 per application, up to 2]. Limitations — large-scale production is still expensive and difficult, properties in bulk differ from individual sheets, and other recently isolated materials (e.g. other 2D materials) are also significant [1 per valid limitation, up to 2]. Justified conclusion — e.g. graphene has outstanding potential but calling it definitively 'most useful' overstates current practical impact [1].
Secure (4–6): Multiple valid points, limited evaluation or conclusion.
Developing (2–3): Some valid properties mentioned, little evaluation.
Emerging (1): Only a single vague property.

lessons.title: Quantitative Chemistry: Moles, Mass and Yield

before.content_html:
What Is a Mole?

A mole is the chemist's counting unit. Just as a dozen always means 12, one mole always contains \(6.02 \times 10^{23}\) particles — whether those particles are atoms, molecules or ions. This enormous number is called Avogadro's constant (\(N_A\)).

The key link between moles and mass is the molar mass. For any element, the molar mass in grams equals its relative atomic mass (\(A_r\)). For compounds, add up the \(A_r\) values of all the atoms in the formula to get the relative formula mass (\(M_r\)).

Key Fact

\[\text{moles} = \frac{\text{mass (g)}}{\text{molar mass (g/mol)}}\] One mole of any element has a mass equal to its relative atomic mass in grams. For CO₂: \(M_r = 12 + (2 \times 16) = 44\,\text{g/mol}\).

Q: Calculate the number of moles in 22 g of carbon dioxide (\(CO_2\), \(M_r = 44\)).

Step 1 — Find \(M_r\): \(12 + (2 \times 16) = 44\,\text{g/mol}\).

Step 2 — Apply the formula: \(\text{moles} = \frac{22}{44} = 0.5\,\text{mol}\).

Q: What mass of sodium hydroxide (NaOH, \(M_r = 40\)) contains 0.25 mol?

Rearrange: \(\text{mass} = \text{moles} \times M_r = 0.25 \times 40 = 10\,\text{g}\).

Using Moles in Balanced Equations

A balanced chemical equation shows the molar ratio of reactants to products. For example:

$$2\,Mg + O_2 \rightarrow 2\,MgO$$

The numbers in front (coefficients) tell you that 2 moles of magnesium react with 1 mole of oxygen to produce 2 moles of magnesium oxide. To find the mass of a product from a known mass of reactant: (1) calculate moles of reactant, (2) use the ratio to find moles of product, (3) convert moles of product to mass.

Q: What mass of MgO is produced when 12 g of Mg burns completely? (\(A_r\): Mg = 24, O = 16)

Step 1 — Moles of Mg: \(\frac{12}{24} = 0.5\,\text{mol}\).

Step 2 — Ratio from equation: 2 mol Mg : 2 mol MgO → 1:1 ratio, so moles of MgO = 0.5 mol.

Step 3 — Mass of MgO: \(M_r(\text{MgO}) = 24 + 16 = 40\,\text{g/mol}\). Mass \(= 0.5 \times 40 = 20\,\text{g}\).

Limiting Reactants

In most reactions, one reactant runs out before the others. The limiting reactant determines the maximum amount of product. To identify it: calculate the moles of each reactant and compare to the stoichiometric ratio. Whichever reactant would be exhausted first is the limiting reactant; the other is in excess.

Key Fact

The limiting reactant is the one that runs out first. The amount of product formed is always calculated from the moles of the limiting reactant, not the excess reactant.

Percentage Yield

In practice, reactions rarely produce the theoretical maximum amount of product. Some product may be lost during transfer between vessels, some reactions may not go to completion, or unwanted side reactions may occur. The percentage yield compares the actual yield to the theoretical maximum:

$$\text{percentage yield} = \frac{\text{actual yield}}{\text{theoretical yield}} \times 100$$

Industrial chemists aim to maximise percentage yield to reduce waste and cost. Factors lowering yield include incomplete reactions, reversible reactions that reach equilibrium before completion, and losses during filtration or evaporation.

Q: A reaction has a theoretical yield of 50 g of aspirin. The chemist isolates 38 g. Calculate the percentage yield.

\(\text{percentage yield} = \frac{38}{50} \times 100 = 76\%\)

In an industrial context, a 76% yield would be assessed against the cost of raw materials and any waste disposal requirements before deciding if the process is commercially viable.

Atom Economy

Atom economy measures how efficiently a reaction converts reactants into the desired product. Unlike percentage yield (which measures what you got versus what you could get), atom economy is a property of the reaction equation itself:

$$\text{atom economy} = \frac{\text{sum of } M_r \text{ of desired products}}{\text{sum of } M_r \text{ of all products}} \times 100$$

A reaction where all atoms end up in the desired product has an atom economy of 100%. Addition reactions (where everything combines into one product) are ideal. Reactions that produce many by-products have low atom economy and generate chemical waste — an important issue in green chemistry and industrial sustainability.

Key Fact

Atom economy = (\(M_r\) of useful products ÷ \(M_r\) of all products) × 100. High atom economy is desirable — less waste, lower cost, more sustainable. A 100% atom economy means every atom of reactant ends up in the desired product.
before.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • One mole = 6.02 × 10²³ particles. Moles = mass ÷ molar mass (\(M_r\)). \(M_r\) is found by adding up relative atomic masses for all atoms in the formula.
  • Balanced equations give molar ratios. The limiting reactant runs out first and determines the theoretical yield. Percentage yield = (actual ÷ theoretical) × 100.
  • Atom economy = (\(M_r\) of desired products ÷ \(M_r\) of all products) × 100. High atom economy means less waste — important for industrial sustainability and green chemistry.
before.exam_tip_html: The most common calculation error on moles questions is forgetting to divide mass by \(M_r\) — instead students just write down the mass. Always state the equation, substitute values, and give a final answer with units. For percentage yield: the theoretical yield must be calculated via balanced equation first, then divide actual by theoretical and multiply by 100. For atom economy: use the balanced equation and the \(M_r\) values of products only — not reactants. In 6-mark 'describe a method' questions on making a salt, examiners explicitly look for: independent variable, dependent variable, control variables, repeats, and how data will be analysed — missing any of these caps the mark.

practice_questions.text:
Calculate the relative formula mass (Mr) of calcium carbonate (CaCO₃).
(Relative atomic masses: Ca = 40, C = 12, O = 16)
practice_questions.marks: Mr = 40 + 12 + (3 × 16) [1 mark] = 100 [1 mark]. No unit needed for Mr.

practice_questions.text:
Calculate the number of moles in 8.0 g of sulfur dioxide (SO₂).
(Relative atomic masses: S = 32, O = 16)
practice_questions.marks: Mr of SO₂ = 32 + (2 × 16) = 64 [1 mark for Mr]. Moles = 8.0 ÷ 64 = 0.125 mol [1 mark].

practice_questions.text:
In an industrial process, hydrogen and nitrogen react to form ammonia:
N₂ + 3H₂ → 2NH₃
Calculate the mass of ammonia that can be produced from 6.0 g of hydrogen gas.
(Relative atomic masses: H = 1, N = 14)
practice_questions.marks: Mr of H₂ = 2; moles of H₂ = 6.0 ÷ 2 = 3.0 mol [1 mark]. Ratio H₂ : NH₃ = 3 : 2, so moles of NH₃ = 3.0 × (2/3) = 2.0 mol [1 mark]. Mr of NH₃ = 14 + 3 = 17; mass = 2.0 × 17 = 34 g [1 mark].

practice_questions.text: A student carries out a reaction and obtains 18.4 g of product. The theoretical yield is 23.0 g. Calculate the percentage yield.
practice_questions.marks: Percentage yield = (18.4 ÷ 23.0) × 100 [1 mark] = 80% [1 mark].

practice_questions.text: Explain what is meant by atom economy and why a high atom economy is desirable in industrial chemical processes.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (4): Atom economy is the proportion of the mass of reactants that ends up in the desired product [1 mark], calculated as (Mr of desired products ÷ Mr of all products) × 100 [1 mark]. High atom economy means less waste is produced [1 mark], which is more cost-effective (less raw material wasted) and more sustainable/environmentally friendly [1 mark].
Secure (2–3): Correct definition and one benefit.
Developing (1): States it involves products and reactants without a correct definition.

practice_questions.text:
In the reaction: CaCO₃ → CaO + CO₂
Calculate the atom economy for producing calcium oxide (CaO).
(Relative atomic masses: Ca = 40, C = 12, O = 16)
practice_questions.marks: Step 1 — Mr of CaCO₃ = 40 + 12 + (3×16) = 100 [1 mark]. Step 2 — Mr of CaO = 40 + 16 = 56 [1 mark]. Step 3 — Mr of CO₂ = 12 + (2×16) = 44 [1 mark]. Step 4 — Sum of Mr of all products = 56 + 44 = 100 [1 mark]. Step 5 — Atom economy = (56 ÷ 100) × 100 = 56% [1 mark]. Step 6 — Interpretation: 44% of the starting mass becomes CO₂ waste; this is a moderate atom economy and the CO₂ by-product has implications for carbon emissions in industrial lime production [1 mark].

flashcard_questions.a: A counting unit for particles. One mole contains 6.02 × 10²³ particles (Avogadro's constant).
flashcard_questions.q: What is a mole in chemistry?

flashcard_questions.a: Divide the mass in grams by the molar mass (Mr): moles = mass ÷ Mr.
flashcard_questions.q: How do you calculate the number of moles from mass?

flashcard_questions.a: By adding up the relative atomic masses (Ar) of all the atoms in the formula.
flashcard_questions.q: How is the relative formula mass (Mr) of a compound found?

flashcard_questions.a: The reactant that is completely used up first in a reaction, determining the maximum amount of product that can be formed.
flashcard_questions.q: What is the limiting reactant?

flashcard_questions.a: The fraction of the theoretical maximum yield that is actually obtained. Percentage yield = (actual yield ÷ theoretical yield) × 100.
flashcard_questions.q: What is percentage yield and how is it calculated?

flashcard_questions.a: A measure of how much of the reactant mass becomes useful product. Atom economy = (Mr of desired products ÷ Mr of all products) × 100.
flashcard_questions.q: What is atom economy?

flashcard_questions.a: It means less waste is produced — reducing raw material costs and environmental impact.

before.content_html:
The Reactivity Series

Metals can be arranged in order of their chemical reactivity — this is called the reactivity series. From most to least reactive: potassium (K), sodium (Na), calcium (Ca), magnesium (Mg), aluminium (Al), carbon (C), zinc (Zn), iron (Fe), hydrogen (H), copper (Cu), silver (Ag), gold (Au). Carbon and hydrogen are included as non-metal reference points.

A more reactive metal will displace a less reactive metal from a solution of its compound. For example, iron displaces copper from copper(II) sulfate solution:

$$Fe + CuSO_4 \rightarrow FeSO_4 + Cu$$

The solution changes from blue to colourless, and a copper-coloured solid forms on the iron. This is evidence that a displacement reaction has occurred.

Key Fact

Reactivity series (most → least reactive): K, Na, Ca, Mg, Al, C, Zn, Fe, H, Cu, Ag, Au. A more reactive metal displaces a less reactive metal from its compound. Metals above carbon must be extracted by electrolysis; those below carbon can be extracted by reduction with carbon.

Oxidation and Reduction (Redox)

Displacement reactions are redox reactions — one species is oxidised while another is reduced. The memory aid OIL RIG helps keep the definitions straight: Oxidation Is Loss (of electrons), Reduction Is Gain (of electrons).

In the iron/copper sulfate displacement reaction: iron atoms lose electrons to become \(Fe^{2+}\) ions — iron is oxidised. Copper(II) ions gain electrons to become copper atoms — copper is reduced.

Key Fact

OIL RIG — Oxidation Is Loss of electrons, Reduction Is Gain. In displacement reactions, the more reactive metal (higher in the series) is oxidised; the less reactive metal ion is reduced. Both changes happen simultaneously.

Extracting Metals from Their Ores

Most metals are found in the Earth's crust combined with other elements in ores. The method of extraction depends on the metal's position in the reactivity series:

  • Metals less reactive than carbon (e.g. iron, zinc, copper) — extracted by reduction with carbon. Carbon (or carbon monoxide) is more reactive than these metals under smelting conditions, so it removes the oxygen from the metal oxide.
  • Metals more reactive than carbon (e.g. aluminium, sodium, potassium) — must be extracted by electrolysis. This requires large amounts of electricity, making it much more expensive.

Iron is extracted from iron(III) oxide (\(Fe_2O_3\)) in a blast furnace. Coke (carbon) burns in hot air to form carbon dioxide, which then reacts with more coke to form carbon monoxide (CO). The carbon monoxide reduces the iron oxide:

$$Fe_2O_3 + 3CO \rightarrow 2Fe + 3CO_2$$

Limestone (\(CaCO_3\)) is added to remove acidic silicon dioxide impurities as liquid slag (calcium silicate), which is tapped off separately from the molten iron.

Rusting and Corrosion

Rusting occurs when iron or steel is exposed to both water and oxygen. The overall reaction produces hydrated iron(III) oxide (rust). Rusting is an oxidation process — iron is oxidised. Preventing rusting is commercially vital: methods include galvanising (zinc coating), painting, oiling, or using a sacrificial metal (attaching a more reactive metal that corrodes preferentially).

Alloys

A pure metal has a regular lattice of identical atoms that can slide over each other easily, making the metal soft. An alloy contains atoms of different sizes, which distort the lattice and make it harder for layers to slide. This makes alloys harder and stronger than the pure metals they contain.

Steel: iron + carbon (and sometimes other metals). Low-carbon steel is malleable; high-carbon steel is harder and more brittle; stainless steel (iron + chromium + nickel) is corrosion-resistant.

Bronze: copper + tin. Harder than copper alone; used for statues, bells and bearings.

Brass: copper + zinc. Harder than copper; used for musical instruments and decorative fittings.

Gold alloys (carat gold): pure gold is too soft for jewellery; it is alloyed with silver or copper. 18-carat gold contains 18 parts gold in 24 parts alloy (75% gold).

Key Fact

Alloys are harder than pure metals because the different-sized atoms disrupt the regular metallic lattice, preventing layers from sliding easily over each other.

Electroplating uses electrolysis to deposit a thin layer of metal onto an object. The object to be plated acts as the cathode (negative electrode), the plating metal acts as the anode (positive electrode), and both are placed in a solution containing ions of the plating metal. Metal ions are reduced at the cathode and deposited onto the object; the anode gradually dissolves to replenish the ions. Applications include chrome plating of car parts, silver plating of cutlery, and tin plating of steel cans.

before.content_html:
Acids, Bases and the pH Scale

An acid is a substance that produces hydrogen ions (\(H^+\)) when dissolved in water. A base is a substance that neutralises an acid. An alkali is a soluble base — it produces hydroxide ions (\(OH^-\)) when dissolved in water.

The pH scale runs from 0 (most acidic) to 14 (most alkaline), with 7 being exactly neutral. pH is measured using universal indicator (which changes colour) or a pH probe (which gives a precise digital reading).

Key Fact

Acids: produce \(H^+\) ions, pH 0–6. Neutral: pH 7. Alkalis: produce \(OH^-\) ions, pH 8–14. The neutralisation reaction: \(H^+ + OH^- \rightarrow H_2O\).

Neutralisation Reactions

Neutralisation occurs when an acid reacts with a base, producing a salt and water. The key reaction types are:

  • Acid + metal → salt + hydrogen gas. E.g. \(Mg + H_2SO_4 \rightarrow MgSO_4 + H_2\)
  • Acid + metal oxide → salt + water. E.g. \(CuO + H_2SO_4 \rightarrow CuSO_4 + H_2O\)
  • Acid + metal hydroxide → salt + water. E.g. \(NaOH + HCl \rightarrow NaCl + H_2O\)
  • Acid + metal carbonate → salt + water + carbon dioxide. E.g. \(CaCO_3 + 2HCl \rightarrow CaCl_2 + H_2O + CO_2\)

The name of the salt produced depends on the acid used: hydrochloric acid (HCl) makes chlorides, sulfuric acid (\(H_2SO_4\)) makes sulfates, and nitric acid (\(HNO_3\)) makes nitrates.

Key Fact

HCl → chlorides. \(H_2SO_4\) → sulfates. \(HNO_3\) → nitrates. Salt name = metal name + acid ending. Example: sodium + sulfuric acid → sodium sulfate.

Making Pure Dry Salts

To make copper(II) sulfate crystals from copper(II) oxide and sulfuric acid (a core practical):

  1. Warm dilute sulfuric acid in a beaker.
  2. Add excess copper(II) oxide (black powder) and stir until no more dissolves — the excess ensures all acid is used up.
  3. Filter the mixture to remove the excess copper(II) oxide.
  4. Evaporate the blue filtrate gently until crystals begin to form, then leave to crystallise fully.
  5. Pat the blue crystals dry with filter paper.

The independent variable is the amount of acid used; the thermometer measures temperature (it does not control it — the water bath controls temperature).

Some salts are insoluble and cannot be made by neutralisation. They are made by precipitation: mix two solutions whose ions react to form the insoluble salt. For example, to make barium sulfate: mix barium chloride solution with sodium sulfate solution — barium sulfate precipitates immediately. Filter, wash with distilled water and dry.

$$BaCl_2 + Na_2SO_4 \rightarrow BaSO_4 + 2NaCl$$

Titration

Titration is used to find the exact volume of acid needed to neutralise a known volume of alkali (or vice versa). The apparatus required includes a burette (to deliver the acid) and a pipette (to measure the exact volume of alkali). An indicator such as phenolphthalein or methyl orange shows when the endpoint is reached.

1. Rinse the burette with the acid solution, then fill it and record the initial reading to 0.05 cm³. 2. Use the pipette to measure an exact volume of alkali into a conical flask; add a few drops of indicator. 3. Add the acid from the burette drop by drop, swirling the flask. As the endpoint approaches, add half-drops. 4. Stop when the indicator changes colour permanently. Record the final burette reading. 5. Calculate the volume added (titre = final − initial). Repeat until two titres agree within 0.10 cm³; these are concordant results. Average the concordant results.

From a titration, use: \(n = c \times V\) where \(n\) = moles, \(c\) = concentration (mol/dm³), \(V\) = volume (dm³). Convert cm³ to dm³ by dividing by 1000.

Example: 25.0 cm³ of NaOH solution of concentration 0.10 mol/dm³ required 20.0 cm³ of HCl solution. Find the concentration of the HCl.

Moles NaOH \(= 0.10 \times 0.025 = 0.0025\) mol. From NaOH + HCl → NaCl + H₂O, the ratio is 1:1, so moles HCl = 0.0025 mol. Concentration HCl \(= \frac{0.0025}{0.020} = 0.125\) mol/dm³.

A key distinction for the exam is between strong and weak acids: strength refers to the degree of ionisation in water, not concentration. A concentrated weak acid like ethanoic acid has a lower pH than a dilute weak acid, but both ionise only partially. When making soluble salts by neutralisation, use an indicator to find the exact equivalence point; when using an insoluble base, add excess and then filter to remove it — no indicator is needed because the excess base is simply removed by filtration.
before.exam_tip_html: On 6-mark 'describe a method' questions for making a soluble salt, examiners want: (1) add excess insoluble base to the acid; (2) filter to remove excess solid; (3) evaporate gently and crystallise. Crucially, a thermometer in the experiment measures temperature — the water bath controls it. Mixing these up is the most common mark loss in core practical questions. For titration calculations: always convert cm³ to dm³ before using \(n = c \times V\). Concordant results means two titres that agree within 0.10 cm³ — the anomalous (rough) result is excluded from the average.

before.content_html:
What Is Electrolysis?

Electrolysis is the process of using an electric current to break down an ionic compound. The compound being broken down is called the electrolyte, and it must be either molten or dissolved so that the ions are free to move.

The electrolyte is connected to two solid conductors called electrodes. The cathode is the negative electrode; the anode is the positive electrode. The memory aid PANIC helps: Positive Anode, Negative Is Cathode.

Key Fact

Electrolysis: positive ions (cations) move to the cathode (negative) and gain electrons — this is reduction. Negative ions (anions) move to the anode (positive) and lose electrons — this is oxidation. PANIC: Positive Anode, Negative Is Cathode.

Electrolysis of Molten Ionic Compounds

When a molten ionic compound is electrolysed, only the ions from that compound are present. For molten lead(II) bromide (\(PbBr_2\)):

  • Cathode: \(Pb^{2+}\) ions gain electrons → lead metal deposited. \(Pb^{2+} + 2e^- \rightarrow Pb\)
  • Anode: \(Br^-\) ions lose electrons → bromine gas released. \(2Br^- \rightarrow Br_2 + 2e^-\)

These equations showing what happens at each electrode are called half-equations. The electrons lost at the anode must equal the electrons gained at the cathode.

Electrolysis of Aqueous Solutions

When an ionic compound is dissolved in water, \(H^+\) and \(OH^-\) ions from water are also present. This means there is competition at each electrode between different ions:

At the cathode:

  • If the metal cation is less reactive than hydrogen (e.g. Cu²⁺, Ag⁺) → the metal is deposited.
  • If the metal cation is more reactive than hydrogen (e.g. Na⁺, Zn²⁺) → hydrogen gas is produced instead.

At the anode:

  • If a halide ion is present (Cl⁻, Br⁻, I⁻) → the halogen is produced (e.g. chlorine gas).
  • If no halide is present → oxygen is produced from the discharge of \(OH^-\) ions.

Aluminium Extraction by Electrolysis

Aluminium is too reactive to be extracted by reduction with carbon, so it is extracted by electrolysis of molten aluminium oxide (\(Al_2O_3\)).

Pure aluminium oxide has a very high melting point (over 2000 °C). To reduce energy costs, it is dissolved in molten cryolite, which lowers the melting point to around 950 °C.

Key Fact

Aluminium extraction: electrolysis of \(Al_2O_3\) dissolved in molten cryolite (lowers melting point). At cathode: \(Al^{3+} + 3e^- \rightarrow Al\). At anode: oxygen released reacts with the carbon anodes, burning them away — they need regular replacement.

Cathode (reduction): \(Al^{3+} + 3e^- \rightarrow Al\)

Anode (oxidation): \(2O^{2-} \rightarrow O_2 + 4e^-\)

The oxygen produced at the anode reacts with the carbon (graphite) anodes at high temperature, forming carbon dioxide. This means the anodes gradually burn away and must be replaced regularly — a significant running cost.

Core Practical: Electrolysis of Copper Sulfate Solution

This core practical investigates the electrolysis of aqueous copper sulfate solution, comparing the effect of inert electrodes (carbon) versus active electrodes (copper).

With inert (carbon) electrodes:

  • Cathode: copper metal deposits (Cu²⁺ + 2e⁻ → Cu). The cathode gains mass.
  • Anode: oxygen gas is produced (no halide present). The copper sulfate solution gradually becomes paler as Cu²⁺ ions are removed.

With copper electrodes (active):

  • Cathode: copper still deposits — cathode gains mass.
  • Anode: the copper anode dissolves (Cu → Cu²⁺ + 2e⁻). The anode loses mass. The Cu²⁺ concentration in solution remains roughly constant, making this the basis of copper purification and electroplating.

To test the gas at the anode: a glowing splint would relight if it were oxygen. To test for copper, observe the reddish-brown deposit at the cathode. Weigh the electrodes before and after to quantify mass changes.

Common Misconceptions and Exam Pitfalls

A frequent error is assuming that the positive electrode always produces oxygen — this only applies when no halide ions (such as chloride) are present in solution. When chloride ions are present in higher concentration, chlorine gas forms at the anode instead. Likewise, students sometimes confuse electrolytic cells with electrochemical cells: in an electrolytic cell, electrical energy is put in to drive a non-spontaneous chemical change, whereas in a galvanic cell, chemical energy is converted out to electrical energy. Always identify the type of electrode material and the ions present in solution before predicting products.

practice_questions.marks:

Half-equation: 2H⁺ + 2e⁻ → H₂ [1 mark]. At the anode — Cl⁻ ions are present (a halide), so chlorine gas is produced preferentially rather than oxygen [1 mark]. Half-equation: 2Cl⁻ → Cl₂ + 2e⁻ [1 mark]. Observation: chlorine bleaches damp litmus paper; hydrogen burns with a squeaky pop [1 mark].

Developing (1–2): States 'hydrogen and chlorine' without explaining the discharge rules.

knowledge_checks.q: Which statement correctly describes an endothermic reaction?
options: Energy is released to the surroundings and temperature rises.

left: Combustion of methane

practice_questions.text: Explain the difference between an exothermic and an endothermic reaction in terms of energy transfer to or from the surroundings.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Clearly distinguishes both types by direction of energy transfer; links to bond breaking (endothermic) and bond making (exothermic); explains why temperature of surroundings rises or falls; includes precise scientific vocabulary throughout.
Secure: States direction of energy transfer for both types; explains temperature change; may not fully develop bond-energy reasoning.
Developing: Identifies one type correctly with temperature change; explanation of the other is partial or missing.
Emerging: Names one type with limited or no explanation of energy transfer.

practice_questions.text: The table below gives bond energies for the reaction: \(N_2 + 3H_2 \rightarrow 2NH_3\). Bond energies: N≡N = 945 kJ/mol; H–H = 436 kJ/mol; N–H = 391 kJ/mol. Calculate the overall energy change for this reaction. Show your working clearly and give the sign and units in your answer.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark: correct energy to break bonds (945 + 3 × 436 = 2253 kJ/mol). 1 mark: correct energy released making bonds (6 × 391 = 2346 kJ/mol). 1 mark: correct overall change with sign and units (ΔH = 2253 − 2346 = −93 kJ/mol, exothermic). ECF applies if arithmetic error in step 1 or 2.

practice_questions.text: Describe what is shown by an exothermic reaction profile, including how the activation energy and overall energy change are represented on the diagram.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark: reactants at higher energy level than products. 1 mark: activation energy is the height from reactant energy level to the peak. 1 mark: overall energy change is the difference in height between reactants and products, with energy released shown as a downward arrow or negative value.

practice_questions.text: State what is meant by activation energy.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark: the minimum energy that reacting particles must have (possess / collide with) for a reaction to occur (for a collision to be successful).

practice_questions.text: A student uses bond energies to calculate the energy change for a reaction and gets +250 kJ/mol. State whether the reaction is exothermic or endothermic. Explain what this value tells you about the bond energies involved.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark: endothermic. 1 mark: the energy needed to break the bonds in the reactants is greater than the energy released when bonds form in the products (by 250 kJ/mol).

practice_questions.text: Explain how a catalyst increases the rate of a reaction. In your answer, refer to activation energy and reaction profiles.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Explains that catalyst provides an alternative reaction pathway; lower activation energy means a greater proportion of collisions have sufficient energy; links to rate profile showing lower peak; notes overall energy change is unchanged.
Secure: States catalyst lowers activation energy; links to more successful collisions; may not mention unchanged overall energy change.
Developing: States catalyst lowers activation energy without linking to collision frequency or the profile.
Emerging: States catalyst speeds up reaction without reference to activation energy or energy profiles.

before.exam_tip_html: In bond energy calculations, show your working in three labelled steps (bonds broken, bonds made, overall change) and include the sign: a positive ΔH is endothermic, a negative ΔH is exothermic. Missing units (kJ/mol) or the sign will cost a mark.
